With speed comes risk. Also, a circuit's speed will generally increase as more rubber gets laid down into it. All other things being equal, that makes the end of the session the best condition to put the fastest possible lap in. In qualifying, it's much better to put in a 'banker' lap at, say, 80 or 90% in order to have a time recorded than to only wait until the end of the session to do the 100% lap. Also, changing conditions can negatively affect the circuit's speed (track temp, wind gusts, rain,) and it's always possible to have an incident causing yellow flags or red flags. Putting in a 'banker' lap allows the team to mitigate those risks without too much at stake (generally just a set of tires.)

They fitted larger wheels, but that then meant that they couldn't use the bespoke tyres made for them to handle the huge amount of acceleration, braking, and turning that their fronts have to do. One advancement of modern engines is reducing the time to warm up the engine. Cold engines have cold oil, which don't lubricate as well. The faster the car warms up, the faster the oil gets to a temperature where it can fully protect all of the moving parts inside the engine, and also, the faster the catalytic converter warms up and starts being effective at reducing tailpipe emissions. The cold oil problem is why it's a bad idea to ask a lot of your engine when its cold (either by lots of engine load or high revs or both.) I don't know what specific advances lead to raising the engine (and thus oil) temperature quickly, but one progression that has happened from the catalytic converter perspective is moving the catalyst ever closer to the engine cylinders themselves.
